blocks.en: "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to Your lovingkindness; according to the multitude of Your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions." — Psalm 51:1 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Ten piedad de mí, oh Dios, conforme a tu misericordia; conforme a la multitud de tus piedades borra mis rebeliones." — Salmo 51:1 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. A Sickness No Doctor Can Cure
blocks.es_reference: 1. Una Enfermedad que Ningún Médico Puede Curar

blocks.en: There is a kind of sickness for which doctors have no cure. It is spiritual sickness, and it was the sickness King David carried for more than a year. David had sinned with Bathsheba and then had her husband Uriah killed to cover it up. For an entire year he was separated from God, and you can imagine how miserable he was during that time. He broke up a home; he committed adultery and murder. And yet this same man is called one of the greatest who ever lived — a man after God's own heart. How can both things be true? Because the story of Psalm 51 is not finally about a man's sin; it is about how a sinner finds his way home to God.
blocks.es_reference: Hay una clase de enfermedad para la cual los médicos no tienen cura. Es la enfermedad espiritual, y fue la enfermedad que el rey David cargó por más de un año. David había pecado con Betsabé y luego hizo matar a su esposo Urías para encubrirlo. Por un año entero estuvo separado de Dios, y puede imaginar cuán miserable fue durante ese tiempo. Destruyó un hogar; cometió adulterio y homicidio. Y sin embargo a este mismo hombre se le llama uno de los más grandes que jamás vivieron — un hombre conforme al corazón de Dios. ¿Cómo pueden ser ciertas ambas cosas? Porque la historia del Salmo 51 no trata al final del pecado de un hombre; trata de cómo un pecador halla el camino de regreso a Dios.

blocks.en: One day David's preacher came to see him. His name was Nathan, a prophet of God — the kind of pastor who visited his members. The 51st Psalm is the prayer David wrote out of that visit. In it we can watch, step by step, exactly how a guilty man returns to the God he has wronged. There are four steps, and they are the same four steps every one of us must take.
blocks.es_reference: Un día el predicador de David vino a verlo. Su nombre era Natán, un profeta de Dios — de esos pastores que visitan a sus miembros. El Salmo 51 es la oración que David escribió a raíz de esa visita. En él podemos observar, paso a paso, exactamente cómo un hombre culpable regresa al Dios a quien ha agraviado. Hay cuatro pasos, y son los mismos cuatro pasos que cada uno de nosotros debe dar.

blocks.en: 2. David Was Confronted with His Sin
blocks.es_reference: 2. David Fue Confrontado con su Pecado

blocks.en: Psalm 51:1-2 (NKJV): "Have mercy upon me, O God, according to Your lovingkindness; according to the multitude of Your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 51:1-2 (RVG): "Ten piedad de mí, oh Dios, conforme a tu misericordia; conforme a la multitud de tus piedades borra mis rebeliones. Lávame más y más de mi maldad, y límpiame de mi pecado."

blocks.en: The prophet had probably known about the sin for some time, but he said nothing until God sent him. Nathan understood the danger; throughout history messengers who brought bad news were often killed, and David held the power of life and death over him. So the man of God came and told a story: a rich man with many flocks took the one little ewe lamb of a poor man and killed it for a guest. David was furious. "Such a man should be put to death!" Then Nathan looked at his king and said, "You are the man." David, the rich king with many wives, had taken Uriah's wife and then had Uriah murdered. He had condemned himself.
blocks.es_reference: El profeta probablemente había sabido del pecado por algún tiempo, pero no dijo nada hasta que Dios lo envió. Natán comprendía el peligro; a lo largo de la historia los mensajeros que traían malas noticias a menudo eran matados, y David tenía poder de vida y muerte sobre él. Así que el hombre de Dios vino y contó una historia: un hombre rico con muchos rebaños tomó la única corderita de un hombre pobre y la mató para un huésped. David se enfureció. "¡Tal hombre debe morir!" Entonces Natán miró a su rey y dijo: "Tú eres aquel hombre." David, el rey rico con muchas esposas, había tomado a la esposa de Urías y luego había hecho matar a Urías. Se había condenado a sí mismo.

blocks.en: God is always working to confront us with our sin. Sometimes the Holy Spirit speaks through our conscience, sometimes through the hardships of life, sometimes through a Christian friend. In the parable of the prodigal son, the young man "came to himself" while starving among the pigs, and only then turned home. The first step toward being forgiven is simply to realize that we need forgiveness.
blocks.es_reference: Dios siempre está obrando para confrontarnos con nuestro pecado. A veces el Espíritu Santo habla por medio de nuestra conciencia, a veces por las dificultades de la vida, a veces por un amigo cristiano. En la parábola del hijo pródigo, el joven "volvió en sí" mientras se moría de hambre entre los cerdos, y solo entonces regresó a casa. El primer paso hacia el perdón es simplemente darnos cuenta de que necesitamos perdón.

blocks.en: 3. David Admitted His Sin
blocks.es_reference: 3. David Admitió su Pecado

blocks.en: David cried out, "I have sinned against the LORD." Even though he had wronged Bathsheba and Uriah and the nation, he understood that ultimately he had sinned against God. How differently we usually react when we are told we are sinners, for it is always hard to accept personal responsibility. Consider the easier roads David did not take.
blocks.es_reference: David clamó: "Contra Jehová he pecado." Aunque había agraviado a Betsabé, a Urías y a la nación, comprendió que en última instancia había pecado contra Dios. Cuán diferente solemos reaccionar cuando se nos dice que somos pecadores, pues siempre es difícil aceptar la responsabilidad personal. Considere los caminos más fáciles que David no tomó.

blocks.en: He could have lied: "You have no proof; you don't know what I've done." A small child quickly learns that lying is easier than telling the truth. He could have blamed someone else: that Bathsheba enticed him. That is the oldest excuse there is — when God confronted Adam, his first defense was, "This woman You gave me caused me to do it." He could have made excuses: that he was distracted running the government, or that he had a hard boyhood. He could even have grown angry and had Nathan killed for his insolence.
blocks.es_reference: Pudo haber mentido: "No tienes pruebas; no sabes lo que he hecho." Un niño pequeño aprende pronto que mentir es más fácil que decir la verdad. Pudo haber culpado a otro: que Betsabé lo sedujo. Esa es la excusa más antigua que existe — cuando Dios confrontó a Adán, su primera defensa fue: "Esta mujer que me diste me hizo hacerlo." Pudo haber puesto excusas: que estaba distraído gobernando, o que tuvo una niñez difícil. Pudo incluso haberse enojado y mandado matar a Natán por su insolencia.

blocks.en: Instead of all these, David admitted his sin, because no excuse could suffice. The all-knowing God looks directly into a man's heart and cannot be deceived. He knows our open sins and our secret sins, our sins of commission and our sins of omission. The One who counts the hairs of our head knows about our sins. David was helpless and knew it. The heart that had been frozen for a year was finally thawed, and with a broken spirit he confessed.
blocks.es_reference: En lugar de todo esto, David admitió su pecado, porque ninguna excusa podía bastar. El Dios que todo lo sabe mira directamente al corazón del hombre y no puede ser engañado. Conoce nuestros pecados abiertos y nuestros pecados secretos, nuestros pecados de comisión y nuestros pecados de omisión. Aquel que cuenta los cabellos de nuestra cabeza sabe de nuestros pecados. David estaba indefenso y lo sabía. El corazón que había estado congelado por un año al fin se deshizo, y con espíritu quebrantado confesó.

blocks.en: 4. David Was Sorry for His Sin
blocks.es_reference: 4. David Tuvo Tristeza por su Pecado

blocks.en: The 51st Psalm begins with David begging God to turn his life around. For too long he had been separated from God; for too long he had struggled in guilt and shame; for too long he had been the most miserable of men. It is a sad fact that as long as our lives are caught up in willful sin, we cut ourselves off from God's presence. One of the chief reasons for unanswered prayer is unconfessed sin. Rebellion against God never makes us happy. As long as we know what is right and refuse to do it, we manufacture our own grief.
blocks.es_reference: El Salmo 51 comienza con David rogando a Dios que cambie su vida. Por demasiado tiempo había estado separado de Dios; por demasiado tiempo había luchado en culpa y vergüenza; por demasiado tiempo había sido el más miserable de los hombres. Es un hecho triste que mientras nuestras vidas estén atrapadas en el pecado voluntario, nos apartamos de la presencia de Dios. Una de las principales razones de la oración sin respuesta es el pecado no confesado. La rebelión contra Dios nunca nos hace felices. Mientras sepamos lo que es correcto y rehusemos hacerlo, fabricamos nuestra propia aflicción.

blocks.en: Perhaps the teenage years are the classic years of rebellion. I remember reaching that age and thinking I could make all my own decisions — I did not want anyone telling me when to study, when to come home, or what to choose. Eventually I rebelled against God too, and decided the church was not all that important to me. It took several years to learn that doing whatever I wanted was not as good as it was supposed to be; in fact it was the most miserable time of my life. Perhaps God allows us to hit rock bottom so that we will have nowhere else to look but up. And then He stands waiting for us with open arms.
blocks.es_reference: Quizá los años de la adolescencia son los años clásicos de la rebelión. Recuerdo llegar a esa edad y pensar que podía tomar todas mis propias decisiones — no quería que nadie me dijera cuándo estudiar, cuándo volver a casa, o qué escoger. Con el tiempo me rebelé también contra Dios, y decidí que la iglesia no era tan importante para mí. Me tomó varios años aprender que hacer lo que yo quería no era tan bueno como se suponía; de hecho fue la época más miserable de mi vida. Quizá Dios permite que toquemos fondo para que no tengamos a dónde mirar sino hacia arriba. Y entonces Él nos espera con los brazos abiertos.

blocks.en: 5. David Turned from His Sin
blocks.es_reference: 5. David se Apartó de su Pecado

blocks.en: The 51st Psalm makes clear that David vowed to commit his life to the Lord. Some people think the past, once done, can never be addressed — "what I have written, I have written." It is true we cannot change the past. There is no time machine to undo our mistakes; the record of our lives is written in indelible ink. Lady Macbeth tried in vain to wash the bloodstain from her hands, but the spot remained. And it is true that we can never clear our own consciences. Every sin is ultimately against God, so if we are to be forgiven, God must forgive us.
blocks.es_reference: El Salmo 51 deja claro que David prometió consagrar su vida al Señor. Algunos piensan que el pasado, una vez hecho, jamás puede tratarse — "lo que he escrito, escrito está." Es cierto que no podemos cambiar el pasado. No hay máquina del tiempo para deshacer nuestros errores; el registro de nuestra vida está escrito con tinta indeleble. Lady Macbeth intentó en vano lavar la mancha de sangre de sus manos, pero la mancha permaneció. Y es cierto que nunca podemos limpiar nuestra propia conciencia. Todo pecado es en última instancia contra Dios, así que si hemos de ser perdonados, Dios debe perdonarnos.

blocks.en: Here is the good news: the Bible is the only book of religion that says God completely forgives. When we ask humbly, "Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner," His reply is, "I will remember your sins no more." Yet turning is more than feeling sorry. Zacchaeus the tax collector, when he met Jesus, did not merely confess; he paid back four times what he had stolen. Part of true repentance is the positive act of trying to make our wrongs right. And there is one more thing we can do: we can change the future. There is no real repentance if we are content to keep sinning. At this very moment you are becoming the person you will be in a year; we never stand still — we are always moving toward God or away from Him.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí están las buenas nuevas: la Biblia es el único libro de religión que dice que Dios perdona por completo. Cuando pedimos con humildad: "Señor, ten misericordia de mí, pecador," Su respuesta es: "Nunca más me acordaré de tus pecados." Pero apartarse es más que sentir tristeza. Zaqueo el publicano, al encontrarse con Jesús, no solo confesó; devolvió cuatro veces lo que había robado. Parte del verdadero arrepentimiento es el acto positivo de tratar de enmendar nuestros males. Y hay algo más que podemos hacer: podemos cambiar el futuro. No hay verdadero arrepentimiento si nos contentamos con seguir pecando. En este mismo momento usted se está convirtiendo en la persona que será dentro de un año; nunca estamos quietos — siempre nos movemos hacia Dios o nos alejamos de Él.

blocks.en: 6. The Father Who Runs to Meet Us
blocks.es_reference: 6. El Padre que Corre a Recibirnos

blocks.en: Flora Campbell Comes Home: Ian Maclaren tells of Lachlan Campbell, a stern, cold man who loved his daughter Flora, though her mother had died. Because her father lacked all compassion, Flora ran away from home. Rumors came back of the sinful life she had fallen into, and one day Lachlan struck her name from the family Bible and moved at church that it be dropped from the roll. The congregation refused to act without further study. The next week a kind woman, Margie Howe, went to see him, told him the story of the prodigal son, and finally persuaded him to write to Flora: "Lassie, come home, for your old father is grieving for you. Come home for your sake, for your father's sake, and for the dear Lord's sake." Flora, sick in body and heart, came at once. The next week Margie found written in the family Bible, in the trembling hand of an old man: "Flora Campbell — she went away in May, but she came back in December, and her father fell upon her neck and kissed her." How much more gladly will God receive us back.
blocks.es_reference: Flora Campbell Vuelve a Casa: Ian Maclaren cuenta de Lachlan Campbell, un hombre severo y frío que amaba a su hija Flora, aunque la madre de ella había muerto. Porque su padre carecía de toda compasión, Flora huyó de casa. Llegaron rumores de la vida pecaminosa en que había caído, y un día Lachlan borró su nombre de la Biblia familiar y propuso en la iglesia que se quitara del registro. La congregación se negó a actuar sin más estudio. La semana siguiente una mujer bondadosa, Margie Howe, fue a verlo, le contó la historia del hijo pródigo, y al fin lo persuadió de escribir a Flora: "Muchacha, vuelve a casa, porque tu viejo padre está afligido por ti. Vuelve por tu bien, por el bien de tu padre, y por el bien del Señor amado." Flora, enferma de cuerpo y de corazón, vino enseguida. La semana siguiente Margie halló escrito en la Biblia familiar, con la mano temblorosa de un anciano: "Flora Campbell — se fue en mayo, pero volvió en diciembre, y su padre se echó sobre su cuello y la besó." Cuánto más gozoso nos recibirá Dios de regreso.

blocks.en: 7. The Slate Wiped Clean
blocks.es_reference: 7. La Cuenta Borrada

blocks.en: 1 John 1:9 (NKJV): "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
blocks.es_reference: 1 Juan 1:9 (RVG): "Si confesamos nuestros pecados, él es fiel y justo para perdonar nuestros pecados, y limpiarnos de toda maldad."

blocks.en: David's life was spared through his repentance, but Nathan warned him that "the sword shall never depart from your house." The sin was forgiven, yet consequences remained; any sin leaves certain scars. But here we have an advantage David did not fully see: Christ bore the pain of our sin on the cross.
blocks.es_reference: La vida de David fue perdonada por su arrepentimiento, pero Natán le advirtió que "la espada no se apartará jamás de tu casa." El pecado fue perdonado, pero las consecuencias permanecieron; todo pecado deja ciertas cicatrices. Pero aquí tenemos una ventaja que David no vio del todo: Cristo llevó el dolor de nuestro pecado en la cruz.

blocks.en: "He Doesn't Remember": A pastor had sinned badly, and even though he had confessed it, he never felt forgiven. A woman in his church was always saying, "The Lord said to me …" She was usually right, but it irked him. One day he challenged her: "If God is really speaking to you, ask Him to tell you what sin I committed years ago." A few days later she returned. "Did you ask Him?" he demanded. "Yes," she said. "And what did He say?" The woman answered, "He said He doesn't remember." That is what it means to be forgiven: God blots out the transgression and remembers it no more.
blocks.es_reference: "Él No lo Recuerda": Un pastor había pecado gravemente, y aunque lo había confesado, nunca se sintió perdonado. Una mujer en su iglesia siempre decía: "El Señor me dijo …" Por lo general acertaba, pero a él le molestaba. Un día la desafió: "Si Dios de veras te habla, pídele que te diga qué pecado cometí hace años." Días después ella regresó. "¿Le preguntaste?" exigió él. "Sí," dijo ella. "¿Y qué dijo?" La mujer respondió: "Dijo que no lo recuerda." Eso es lo que significa ser perdonado: Dios borra la transgresión y no la recuerda más.

blocks.en: 8. The Disease and the Only Cure
blocks.es_reference: 8. La Enfermedad y la Única Cura

blocks.en: All through the Bible, sin is pictured as a disease — a terrible disease that is always fatal, and every one of us carries it. As Romans 3:23 says, "all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." The disease is fatal, but there is one cure: Jesus died on the cross to forgive our sins. No matter what they are, we can be forgiven; we are given a second chance.
blocks.es_reference: Por toda la Biblia, el pecado se presenta como una enfermedad — una enfermedad terrible que siempre es mortal, y cada uno de nosotros la lleva. Como dice Romanos 3:23: "por cuanto todos pecaron, y están destituidos de la gloria de Dios." La enfermedad es mortal, pero hay una cura: Jesús murió en la cruz para perdonar nuestros pecados. No importa cuáles sean, podemos ser perdonados; se nos da una segunda oportunidad.

blocks.en: A small boy came through a delicate emergency operation and was breathing freely, but late that night a frightened nurse neglected her duty, and the boy died. The doctor decided she could not be trusted and wrote a letter to end her career. He called her in and read it; she listened in shame and misery. "Have you nothing to say?" he asked. She shook her head, and when she finally spoke she said only, "Give me another chance." That is the cry of every sinner, and the wonder of the gospel is that God grants it. David was confronted, he admitted, he was sorry, and he turned — and instead of punishment he received the forgiveness of God. The same mercy waits for you. Have mercy upon me, O God; blot out my transgressions.
blocks.es_reference: Un niño pequeño salió de una delicada operación de emergencia y respiraba con normalidad, pero ya entrada la noche una enfermera asustada descuidó su deber, y el niño murió. El médico decidió que no se podía confiar en ella y escribió una carta para terminar su carrera. La llamó y se la leyó; ella escuchó con vergüenza y angustia. "¿No tienes nada que decir?" preguntó él. Ella negó con la cabeza, y cuando al fin habló solo dijo: "Deme otra oportunidad." Ese es el clamor de todo pecador, y la maravilla del evangelio es que Dios lo concede. David fue confrontado, admitió, tuvo tristeza, y se apartó — y en lugar de castigo recibió el perdón de Dios. La misma misericordia le espera a usted. Ten piedad de mí, oh Dios; borra mis rebeliones.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what kind of sickness did David carry for more than a year, and which no doctor can cure?
mc.why: David carried a spiritual sickness — the weight of unconfessed sin — that no doctor and no medicine can cure.

mc.stem: What two grievous sins had David committed that lie behind Psalm 51?
options: Adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah
mc.why: Psalm 51 was written after David's two great sins: adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah.

mc.stem: Despite his sin, what is David remarkably called in Scripture?
options: A man after God's own heart
mc.why: Remarkably, even after such sin, David is called a man after God's own heart — because he truly repented.

mc.stem: Who was Nathan, and how does the lesson describe his role?
options: A prophet of God and David's preacher who visited him
mc.why: Nathan was God's prophet and David's preacher, sent to confront the king with his sin.

mc.stem: What are the four steps of David's return to God that structure the lesson?
options: Confronted, admitted, sorry, and turned from his sin
mc.why: The lesson follows David's return in four steps: he was confronted, he admitted, he was sorry, and he turned from his sin.

mc.stem: What story did Nathan tell to confront David, and how did it end?
options: A story of two builders; David praised the wise one
A story of a rich man who took a poor man's lamb; Nathan said, "You are the man"
A story of a lost coin; David rejoiced
A story of a vineyard; David wept
mc.why: Nathan told of a rich man who stole a poor man's lamb, then said, 'You are the man' — and David's guilt was exposed.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, through what means does God confront us with our sin?
options: Through conscience, the hardships of life, and Christian friends
mc.why: God confronts us with our sin through conscience, the hardships of life, and the words of Christian friends.

mc.stem: In the parable of the prodigal son, used in the lesson, what was the first step toward the young man's return?
options: His father came looking for him
He "came to himself" and realized his miserable state
mc.why: The prodigal's return began when he 'came to himself' and honestly faced his miserable state.

mc.stem: When David admitted his sin, what did he cry out?
mc.why: David did not make excuses; he simply cried, 'I have sinned against the LORD' — the heart of true confession.

mc.stem: The lesson lists easier roads David did NOT take. Which is one of them?
options: He could have written a new psalm of praise
He could have blamed Bathsheba or made excuses
He could have fasted for forty days
He could have offered a larger sacrifice
mc.why: David could have blamed Bathsheba or made excuses, but he refused the easier roads and owned his sin.

mc.stem: When God confronted Adam in the garden, what was Adam's first defense — cited as the oldest excuse?
options: "This woman You gave me caused me to do it"
mc.why: Adam's 'this woman You gave me' is the oldest excuse of all — shifting the blame instead of confessing.

mc.stem: Why does the lesson say no excuse could stand before God?
options: Because the all-knowing God looks into the heart and cannot be deceived
mc.why: No excuse can stand because the all-knowing God looks into the heart and cannot be deceived.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what is one of the chief reasons for unanswered prayer?
mc.why: One chief reason for unanswered prayer is unconfessed sin standing between us and God.

mc.stem: In the pastor's personal testimony, what did he learn from his years of rebellion?
options: That doing whatever he wanted was the most miserable time of his life
mc.why: The pastor learned from his years of rebellion that doing whatever he wanted was the most miserable time of his life.

mc.stem: The lesson says turning from sin involves more than feeling sorry. What example shows making wrongs right?
options: Zacchaeus paying back four times what he had stolen
The thief on the cross believing
mc.why: Turning from sin means more than feeling sorry; like Zacchaeus repaying fourfold, it makes wrongs right where it can.

mc.stem: What does the lesson say about our ability to change the past versus the future?
options: We can change the past but not the future
We cannot change the past, but we can change the future
mc.why: We cannot change the past, but by God's grace we can change the future — repentance looks forward.

mc.stem: In Ian Maclaren's story, why did Flora Campbell run away from home?
options: Because her father lacked all compassion and understanding
Because of a famine in the land
Because she was sent away to study
mc.why: Flora ran away because her father lacked all compassion — a picture of how hardness drives the wandering heart away.

mc.stem: Flora Campbell's return to her father is used in the lesson to picture what?
options: That some sins are too great to forgive
That God forgives only after long punishment
That a wandering child should not expect a welcome
The Father's joyful welcome of the repentant sinner who comes home
mc.why: Flora's return pictures the Father's joyful welcome of the repentant sinner who comes home.

mc.stem: In the story of the pastor and the woman who heard from God, what did God reportedly say about the pastor's old sin?
options: That it would be revealed publicly
That the pastor must confess again
mc.why: 'He doesn't remember' shows the wonder of forgiveness: God removes the confessed sin and remembers it no more.

mc.stem: According to the lesson's close, sin is pictured as a fatal disease — and what is the one cure?
options: Jesus dying on the cross to forgive our sins
mc.why: Sin is a fatal disease, and there is only one cure: Jesus dying on the cross to forgive our sins.

sa.prompt: Explain the "spiritual sickness" David carried, and how it shows that Psalm 51 is finally about more than one man's sin.
sa.model: David's "spiritual sickness" was the inner ruin of unconfessed sin: for nearly a year after his sin with Bathsheba he carried guilt that no physician could cure, and it drained the life and joy out of him. Psalm 51 is his cry for healing of the soul. But it is finally about more than one man's failure, because David's sin exposes what is true of us all. Every person carries this same disease of sin and needs the same cleansing. So the psalm becomes a model of repentance for everyone who has ever sinned against God, which is to say, for all of us.

sa.prompt: List and briefly explain the four steps of David's return to God that structure this lesson.
sa.model: The lesson traces David's return to God in four steps. First, he was confronted: God sent Nathan to expose the sin David was hiding. Second, he admitted it, saying plainly, "I have sinned against the LORD," without excuse. Third, he was truly sorry, broken with godly sorrow rather than mere regret at being caught. Fourth, he turned from his sin, seeking to make wrongs right and to live differently going forward. Together these four, confronted, admitted, sorry, and turned, map the path of all genuine repentance.

sa.prompt: How did Nathan confront David, and what does his method teach about how God brings a person to see his own sin?
sa.model: Nathan did not accuse David directly at first; he told a story about a rich man with many flocks who stole and killed a poor man's single beloved lamb. David burned with anger and condemned the rich man to death, at which Nathan said, "You are the man." David had pronounced judgment on himself before he realized it. The method teaches how God brings us to see our own sin: He gets past our defenses, often through conscience, Scripture, or a faithful friend, until we condemn in ourselves what we so easily condemn in others, and the truth finally breaks through.

sa.prompt: According to the lesson, how does God confront us with our sin today? Give the means mentioned.
sa.model: According to the lesson, God confronts us with our sin through several means. He uses our conscience, that inner voice that will not let us rest in wrongdoing. He uses the hardships of life, which can break through our self-satisfaction and turn us back to Him. And He uses Christian friends, who love us enough to speak the truth as Nathan did to David. God is not content to leave us in our sin; in mercy He arranges to confront us, so that we may be brought to repentance and restored before the damage grows worse.

sa.prompt: Describe the easier roads David could have taken instead of admitting his sin, and what he did instead.
sa.model: David could have taken several easier roads. He could have blamed Bathsheba, or made excuses, or covered the sin more deeply as he had already tried to do, or simply used his power as king to silence the matter. Instead he took the hard, honest road: he owned his sin completely, crying, "I have sinned against the LORD," and pleaded for mercy and cleansing. That refusal to excuse himself is the heart of true repentance. The way back to God always runs through honest confession, not through blame-shifting or self-justification.

sa.prompt: Why does willful sin make a person miserable, and how does it relate to unanswered prayer? Use the pastor's testimony.
sa.model: Willful sin makes a person miserable because it sets us against God and against the way we were made to live; the pastor's testimony was that doing whatever he wanted turned out to be the most miserable time of his life. Sin also blocks our fellowship with God, and the lesson notes that unconfessed sin is one of the chief reasons for unanswered prayer; it stands like a wall between us and the Father. The misery and the silence are mercies in disguise, for they drive us back to confession, where joy and answered prayer are restored.

sa.prompt: Explain what it means that David "turned" from his sin, including restitution and changing the future.
sa.model: To say David "turned" from his sin means his repentance was more than feeling sorry; it changed his direction. Turning includes making wrongs right where we can, as Zacchaeus repaid fourfold what he had taken, and it includes a real change in how we live going forward. We cannot undo the past, but by God's grace we can change the future. True repentance is not just grief over yesterday's sin but a deliberate turning of the will toward God for tomorrow, walking a new way rather than the old.

sa.prompt: What does the homecoming of Lachlan and Flora Campbell teach about how God receives the repentant sinner who returns to Him?
sa.model: In Ian Maclaren's story, Flora Campbell ran away from a father who lacked compassion, and for a long time her name was a wound in the home. But when at last she returned, broken, her father ran to meet her, fell on her neck, and received her with joy. It pictures how God receives the repentant sinner who comes home: not with cold reproach but with a Father who runs to welcome us. However far we have wandered, the way back is open, and the Father's heart is set on receiving, forgiving, and restoring the child who returns.

sa.prompt: Using the story of the pastor and the woman who heard from God, explain what it means to be truly forgiven.
sa.model: The story of the pastor and the woman who claimed to hear from God turns on her report of what God said about the pastor's old, confessed sin: "He doesn't remember." That is the wonder of being truly forgiven. When God forgives a confessed sin, He removes it and remembers it against us no more; it no longer stands between us and Him. To be forgiven is not merely to be let off a penalty but to have the sin truly put away, so that the guilt that haunted us is gone. We may remember our sin to stay humble, but God has chosen to forget it.

sa.prompt: The lesson pictures sin as a fatal disease with one cure. Explain the picture and use the "give me another chance" story.
sa.model: The lesson pictures sin as a fatal disease that every person carries and that no human remedy can cure; left untreated it ends in death. There is only one cure: Jesus dying on the cross to take the penalty of our sin and forgive us. The "give me another chance" story shows the heart that finds this cure, the sinner who stops making excuses and pleads for mercy, and receives it. The good news of Psalm 51 is that the disease, though always fatal, is not untreatable; the cross is the cure, and it is offered freely to all who will come.
